title: Actions as Language: Fine-Tuning VLMs into VLAs Without Catastrophic Forgetting
one_liner: Represent robot actions as natural language commands instead of special tokens, so fine-tuning stays inside the language model's trained world and avoids wiping out its reasoning.
lead: When you teach a language model to control a robot, it usually forgets how to reason and understand images. VLM2VLA fixes this by describing robot actions in plain English (like 'move down 5 centimeters and right 2 centimeters') instead of inventing new action codes. This keeps the fine-tuning data close to what the model learned on the internet, so a simple weight adjustment (LoRA) is enough—no need to rebuild the whole model.

problem.h2: The forgetting trap: learning actions breaks reasoning
paras: A vision-language model (a model trained on internet images and text to answer questions and describe things) can be taught to control a robot by fine-tuning on teleoperation data (recordings of a human driving the robot). The problem: learning to predict robot actions wipes out the model's foundational skills. It stops understanding images well, stops following complex instructions, and fails on tasks with objects or words it never saw during robot training.

The naive approach adds special action tokens (new codes for 'move left', 'grasp', etc.) and trains the whole model on robot data. This works for actions, but the model forgets how to reason about the world because the robot data (arm movements, gripper angles) looks nothing like the internet text and images the model was built on. The distribution mismatch—internet scale images plus natural language versus a few thousand robot videos—causes the model to overfit and abandon its earlier knowledge.

callout.html: Write low-level robot actions as natural language sentences, so the fine-tuning data stays close to what the model learned on the internet.

panels.title: 1. The world before
panels.caption: A language model trained on billions of internet images and text. It reasons well.

panels.title: 2. The problem
panels.caption: Add robot action tokens and train on arm data. Model forgets reasoning; weights shift hard.

panels.title: 3. The paper's move
panels.viz_args: Actions as English: 'move down 5cm, right 2cm, grasp'
panels.caption: Write actions as natural language, not new tokens. Stays inside the model's learned world.

panels.title: 4. Gentle updating
panels.caption: LoRA touches only a tiny fraction of weights. Reasoning skills survive; new skills grow.

panels.title: 5. The payoff
panels.caption: Model controls robots AND reasons about new objects and instructions. Both worlds intact.

steps.text: Take each robot action (gripper angle 45 degrees, arm height 12 cm) and describe it as English text ('move up 12 centimeters and rotate gripper to 45 degrees').
The model already knows numbers and spatial words from the internet, so this description feels familiar, not alien.
Instead of retraining the whole model, adjust a small set of extra weights layered on top. The original weights barely move.
Model first generates a high-level subtask in English ('pick up the eggplant'), then a mid-level plan ('move down and left'), then the final action command.
The model stays grounded in reasoning (old internet skills) while learning robot control. Zero-shot transfer to new objects and languages follows.

paras: The paper changes the representation of actions from discrete tokens (new codes invented for each robot command) to natural language descriptions (everyday English sentences that name numbers, directions, and movements). This single change—using words the model already knows instead of new symbols—is what keeps the pretraining distribution intact.

hidden.name: Distance from pretraining
paras: Every fine-tuning step nudges the model away from what it learned on the internet. The more the new data looks different from internet data, the bigger the nudge has to be, and the more the model forgets. The paper measures this indirectly: how well does LoRA work? LoRA is a weak update method—it only works if the new task is close to pretraining. So by comparing LoRA (works well here) to full retraining (needed when data is far), the paper shows it found a way to bring the robot data close to the internet distribution.

The paper validates this by showing that actions-as-language achieves both goals at once: the model's core reasoning abilities stay sharp (tested on Visual Question Answering), and robot control works as well as methods that co-train on internet-scale datasets. That dual success is the proof that the distribution mismatch was truly resolved.

heat.caption: Darker means farther from the model's pretraining. Actions-as-language lives in the light zone.

reads.html: The model learned from the internet where everything is described in words. Robot control data is different (videos and angles). By translating angles into words, the gap shrinks, so the model barely has to change.

The effectiveness of LoRA depends on the fine-tuning distribution being close to pretraining. Representing actions as natural language aligns the VLA data with the VLM's pretrained representations, enabling LoRA-only training without catastrophic forgetting.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: When a model is pretrained on billions of internet examples, it learns the structure of natural language and visual concepts. Its weights are set to predict words in that world. Fine-tuning repoints those weights toward a new task. If the new task looks totally different (raw robot actions, arm angles), the model has to change drastically. LoRA, a parameter-efficient method, makes only small local changes to a few weights—it can only succeed if the new data is close to pretraining.

By representing robot actions in natural language (which the model saw during pretraining), the gap shrinks. The model sees sentences like 'move down 5 centimeters and rotate gripper clockwise'. These words—numbers, directions, objects, verbs—already exist in its pretraining knowledge. So a light touch (LoRA) is enough. The model learns the new action associations while its foundational weights stay stable. This is why reasoning abilities survive and the model can handle unseen tasks: its old skills are still there to ground the reasoning.

math.h2: The equation: balancing stability and adaptation
math.words: Loss is equal to action prediction error plus a small regularization term that steers the model to stay close to its original language-understanding weights.
symbols: how badly the model predicts the robot action
how strongly we protect the original knowledge
the small weight adjustments for layer i

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a layer's action loss is 0.5 (predicting the wrong action slightly).
The LoRA weights in that layer have magnitude 0.3 (small changes so far).
If we tried without actions-as-language, the raw angles would have high action loss (say 2.0) and bigger LoRA weights (say 0.8).
Then penalty would be 2.0 + 0.1 * 0.8^2 = 2.0 + 0.064 = 2.064—the model is forced to change much more.
Actions-as-language keeps the loss small and the weight changes gentle.

math.note: The equation shows that LoRA works only when the action prediction error is small. Natural language actions keep that error small because the model already understands the words.

bars.h2: Before and after: preserving old skills

charts.title: Standard VLA (action tokens + full retraining)
rows: Visual reasoning on internet questions before training
charts.note: Learning actions wipes out reasoning. The model has to choose: understand the world or control the robot, not both.

charts.title: VLM2VLA (actions-as-language + LoRA)
rows: Visual reasoning on internet questions before training
charts.note: Both skills survive. Reasoning barely drops because the model barely changes. Robot control stays strong because actions are now in the model's learned language.

items.html: If the language description of the action is imprecise (e.g., 'move the gripper a bit'), the model cannot ground the words in actual numbers. Performance degrades because the mapping from English to joint angles becomes fuzzy.

items.b: The robot's action space is exotic.
items.html: If the robot does things outside what the model learned from internet text (bizarre arm geometries, continuous morphing tools), no amount of English description helps—there is no pretraining knowledge to anchor to, because the model cannot understand what those motions mean. The words have no grounding.
LoRA adds only a tiny adjustment layer. If the rank (the capacity of that layer) is too small, even staying close to pretraining is not enough—the model simply cannot express new robot skills.

Use precise, numerical language for actions ('move 2.3 centimeters downward, rotate gripper 15 degrees clockwise'). Write out all dimensions the model has seen numbers for during pretraining. Use chain-of-thought (high-level plan first, then action) so the model reasons through the task before outputting actions, which slows down planning but makes it more accurate by grounding the action in the model's language understanding. Test on reasoning tasks to confirm skills survived.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple robot task: grasp a new object (one not in the training data) placed in a new location. Fine-tune a language model on 100 teleoperation examples using the standard method (special action tokens) and also using VLM2VLA (actions as language). Measure two things: (1) Does the model control the robot on the new object? (2) Does it still answer questions about images it was trained on? The demo succeeds when actions-as-language wins on both counts—the baseline picks one or the other.
demo.metric_eq: Reasoning preservation = (accuracy on internet questions after training) / (accuracy before training); Robot control success = (fraction of grasps completed on novel objects)
demo.closing: The single chart that proves the point: one line showing standard method trades reasoning for robot control, another line (actions-as-language) showing both skills intact. The gap is the paper's contribution.
